title: Fossil Record and Rock Layer Evidence Core Test
description: Core practice for interpret fossil placement, rock layers, and anatomical patterns to reason about life history over time.

questions.prompt: In an undisturbed stack of rock layers, where are the oldest fossils usually found?
questions.questionText: In an undisturbed stack of rock layers, where are the oldest fossils usually found?
options: in the lowest layers
in the brightest layers
only in the middle layer
wherever the largest fossil is
questions.correctAnswer: in the lowest layers
questions.explanation: Lower layers are usually older when rock has not been disturbed.

questions.prompt: A fossil shell is found below a fossil fish in undisturbed layers. Which claim is best supported?
questions.questionText: A fossil shell is found below a fossil fish in undisturbed layers. Which claim is best supported?
options: The fish fossil chose to move upward.
The shell fossil must be younger.
Both fossils formed yesterday.
The shell fossil is probably older than the fish fossil.
questions.correctAnswer: The shell fossil is probably older than the fish fossil.
questions.explanation: Layer order gives relative age evidence.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists prefer a pattern of fossils over one fossil?
questions.questionText: Why do scientists prefer a pattern of fossils over one fossil?
options: Patterns remove the need for evidence.
Fossils are unrelated to history.
Patterns across layers provide stronger evidence about change over time.
One fossil always proves every detail.
questions.correctAnswer: Patterns across layers provide stronger evidence about change over time.
questions.explanation: Repeated patterns support stronger claims.

questions.prompt: A rock layer has been folded and tilted. What should scientists do before using layer order?
questions.questionText: A rock layer has been folded and tilted. What should scientists do before using layer order?
options: count only fossil color
check whether the original order has been disturbed
assume the top is always youngest without checking
ignore all fossils
questions.correctAnswer: check whether the original order has been disturbed
questions.explanation: Disturbance can complicate simple layer rules.

questions.prompt: Which model best represents fossil evidence?
questions.questionText: Which model best represents fossil evidence?
options: lower layer -> older fossil -> compare traits with younger fossils
fossil color -> student opinion -> no claim
younger layer -> no organisms ever lived
rock name -> fossil changes by choice
questions.correctAnswer: lower layer -> older fossil -> compare traits with younger fossils
questions.explanation: The model connects layer age to fossil comparison.

questions.prompt: A fossil with fins appears in older layers, and fossils with limb-like bones appear in younger layers. What claim is reasonable?
questions.questionText: A fossil with fins appears in older layers, and fossils with limb-like bones appear in younger layers. What claim is reasonable?
options: Every individual fish grew legs during life.
The younger fossil proves all older fossils are fake.
Layer order never matters.
The fossil record may show a sequence of related body structures over time.
questions.correctAnswer: The fossil record may show a sequence of related body structures over time.
questions.explanation: The claim stays tied to body-structure and layer evidence.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best support a life-history claim?
questions.questionText: Which evidence would best support a life-history claim?
options: a fossil drawn from imagination
the name of the museum gift shop
similar fossils appearing in a consistent order across several locations
one unlabeled rock on a desk
questions.correctAnswer: similar fossils appearing in a consistent order across several locations
questions.explanation: Consistent patterns from multiple places are stronger.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows Layer C at the bottom, Layer B in the middle, and Layer A on top. If undisturbed, which order is oldest to youngest?
questions.questionText: A diagram shows Layer C at the bottom, Layer B in the middle, and Layer A on top. If undisturbed, which order is oldest to youngest?
options: all the same age
C, B, A
A, B, C
B, A, C
questions.correctAnswer: C, B, A
questions.explanation: Bottom-to-top is older-to-younger in undisturbed layers.

questions.prompt: A student says, "Fossils are just guesses." Which response is best?
questions.questionText: A student says, "Fossils are just guesses." Which response is best?
options: Fossils are physical evidence that can be compared with rock-layer patterns.
Fossils never contain evidence.
Guesses are stronger than measurements.
Rock layers cannot be observed.
questions.correctAnswer: Fossils are physical evidence that can be compared with rock-layer patterns.
questions.explanation: Fossils are observable evidence.

questions.prompt: A fossil appears in one layer at three different sites that scientists match as the same age. Why is that useful?
questions.questionText: A fossil appears in one layer at three different sites that scientists match as the same age. Why is that useful?
options: It proves the fossil is alive today.
It removes the need for rock evidence.
It shows all organisms were identical.
It helps compare life evidence across locations.
questions.correctAnswer: It helps compare life evidence across locations.
questions.explanation: Matching layers can connect evidence from different places.

questions.prompt: Which data pattern suggests a trait became more common later in the fossil record?
questions.questionText: Which data pattern suggests a trait became more common later in the fossil record?
options: trait counts were never recorded
only one fossil is shown with no layer
older layers have few fossils with the trait, younger layers have many
all labels are written neatly
questions.correctAnswer: older layers have few fossils with the trait, younger layers have many
questions.explanation: A change in counts across layers is a data pattern.

questions.prompt: Why is relative age different from exact age?
questions.questionText: Why is relative age different from exact age?
options: Older and younger cannot be compared.
Relative age compares older and younger without giving a precise number of years.
Relative age gives a birthday for each fossil.
Exact age means no evidence is needed.
questions.correctAnswer: Relative age compares older and younger without giving a precise number of years.
questions.explanation: Relative age is ordering, not exact dating.

questions.prompt: A younger fossil and older fossil share a similar bone arrangement. What can scientists reasonably infer?
questions.questionText: A younger fossil and older fossil share a similar bone arrangement. What can scientists reasonably infer?
options: The fossils may provide evidence of related structures over time.
The fossils are the same individual.
Bones cannot be compared.
Younger means unrelated by definition.
questions.correctAnswer: The fossils may provide evidence of related structures over time.
questions.explanation: Shared structures can be evidence for relationships.

questions.prompt: What would weaken a fossil-layer claim?
questions.questionText: What would weaken a fossil-layer claim?
options: more fossils from the same pattern
matching layer order at nearby sites
clear labels of top and bottom
evidence that the layers were overturned or faulted
questions.correctAnswer: evidence that the layers were overturned or faulted
questions.explanation: Disturbance can weaken simple age conclusions.

questions.prompt: Which explanation avoids overclaiming?
questions.questionText: Which explanation avoids overclaiming?
options: Layer evidence is never useful.
All fossils are the same age.
The layer pattern supports the claim, but more fossils and dating evidence would strengthen it.
One fossil proves the complete history of life.
questions.correctAnswer: The layer pattern supports the claim, but more fossils and dating evidence would strengthen it.
questions.explanation: Careful science matches claims to evidence.

questions.prompt: A fossil footprint is found, but no bones are found. Is it still fossil evidence?
questions.questionText: A fossil footprint is found, but no bones are found. Is it still fossil evidence?
options: Yes, but it proves exact color.
Yes, traces like footprints can be fossils.
No, only complete skeletons count.
No, footprints are modern drawings.
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, traces like footprints can be fossils.
questions.explanation: Fossils can be traces, not only body remains.

questions.prompt: A table lists fossils from oldest to youngest layers. Trait X appears only in the youngest two layers. Which question should scientists ask next?
questions.questionText: A table lists fossils from oldest to youngest layers. Trait X appears only in the youngest two layers. Which question should scientists ask next?
options: Does the pattern repeat in other locations or more samples?
Can the trait name be shorter?
Which fossil looks funniest?
Can the table be ignored?
questions.correctAnswer: Does the pattern repeat in other locations or more samples?
questions.explanation: More samples test whether the pattern is reliable.

questions.prompt: Which claim best uses evidence?
questions.questionText: Which claim best uses evidence?
options: Fossil A is older because I like its shape.
Fossil B is older because it is smaller.
The fossils have no age relationship.
Because fossil A is below fossil B in undisturbed layers, fossil A is probably older.
questions.correctAnswer: Because fossil A is below fossil B in undisturbed layers, fossil A is probably older.
questions.explanation: The claim names the layer evidence.

questions.prompt: A canyon wall has repeated layers from erosion exposing old rock. Why can it help scientists?
questions.questionText: A canyon wall has repeated layers from erosion exposing old rock. Why can it help scientists?
options: It proves every organism still lives there.
It removes all age evidence.
It shows a sequence of layers that can preserve fossils from different times.
It creates fossils instantly by sunlight.
questions.correctAnswer: It shows a sequence of layers that can preserve fossils from different times.
questions.explanation: Exposed layers can reveal a time sequence.

questions.prompt: Why are missing fossils not surprising?
questions.questionText: Why are missing fossils not surprising?
options: Rocks cannot preserve remains.
Fossil formation requires special conditions, so the record is incomplete.
Every organism always becomes a fossil.
Missing fossils prove no past life existed.
questions.correctAnswer: Fossil formation requires special conditions, so the record is incomplete.
questions.explanation: The fossil record is valuable but incomplete.

questions.prompt: A fossil with a hard shell is common, but soft-bodied fossils are rare. What explanation fits fossilization?
questions.questionText: A fossil with a hard shell is common, but soft-bodied fossils are rare. What explanation fits fossilization?
options: Hard parts are more likely to preserve than soft parts.
Soft bodies never existed.
Hard shells choose to fossilize.
Rock layers dislike soft organisms.
questions.correctAnswer: Hard parts are more likely to preserve than soft parts.
questions.explanation: Preservation depends on materials and conditions.

questions.prompt: Which model is most careful about disturbed layers?
questions.questionText: Which model is most careful about disturbed layers?
options: observe fossils -> ignore disturbance -> claim exact history
choose favorite fossil -> skip layers
count colors -> decide age
observe layer positions -> check for faults or folding -> compare fossils -> make a limited claim
questions.correctAnswer: observe layer positions -> check for faults or folding -> compare fossils -> make a limited claim
questions.explanation: Checking disturbance protects the claim.

questions.prompt: If two fossils are in the same undisturbed layer, what can you infer most directly?
questions.questionText: If two fossils are in the same undisturbed layer, what can you infer most directly?
options: They had identical DNA.
They lived in the same minute.
They are about the same relative age.
They are the same species.
questions.correctAnswer: They are about the same relative age.
questions.explanation: The layer suggests a similar relative age, not identical species or exact time.

questions.prompt: A student says, "Evolution means one fossil turns into the next fossil." What is the best correction?
questions.questionText: A student says, "Evolution means one fossil turns into the next fossil." What is the best correction?
options: Rocks choose which organisms evolve.
Fossils are evidence of populations and related forms over time, not one fossil changing into another.
The statement is exactly correct.
Fossils are never used in evolution.
questions.correctAnswer: Fossils are evidence of populations and related forms over time, not one fossil changing into another.
questions.explanation: Fossils preserve evidence; they do not transform after burial.

questions.prompt: Which evidence combination is strongest?
questions.questionText: Which evidence combination is strongest?
options: layer order, fossil structure comparison, and repeated patterns across sites
favorite fossil, biggest fossil, prettiest fossil
one fossil with no location
a drawing without labels
questions.correctAnswer: layer order, fossil structure comparison, and repeated patterns across sites
questions.explanation: Multiple independent evidence types strengthen the explanation.

questions.prompt: A fossil appears above another fossil after a fault shifted the rock. What should scientists avoid?
questions.questionText: A fossil appears above another fossil after a fault shifted the rock. What should scientists avoid?
options: looking for more evidence
comparing nearby layers
asking whether the fault changed positions
assuming simple top-bottom order without studying the fault
questions.correctAnswer: assuming simple top-bottom order without studying the fault
questions.explanation: Faults can move layers.

questions.prompt: Which data would help estimate a trend in fossil diversity?
questions.questionText: Which data would help estimate a trend in fossil diversity?
options: the number of students in class
whether the fossil name is long
counts of different fossil types in each layer
the color of the notebook
questions.correctAnswer: counts of different fossil types in each layer
questions.explanation: Diversity trends require counts by layer.

questions.prompt: Why is a fossil in younger rock not automatically 'better' than one in older rock?
questions.questionText: Why is a fossil in younger rock not automatically 'better' than one in older rock?
options: Age order is a popularity ranking.
Younger and older describe age, not quality or importance.
Older fossils are never useful.
Younger fossils are always alive.
questions.correctAnswer: Younger and older describe age, not quality or importance.
questions.explanation: Age is evidence, not a value judgment.

questions.prompt: Which final explanation shows strong understanding?
questions.questionText: Which final explanation shows strong understanding?
options: Fossils in ordered rock layers provide evidence for when different forms of life appeared and how patterns changed over time.
Fossils are guesses with no evidence.
Lower rocks are always younger.
One fossil proves every event exactly.
questions.correctAnswer: Fossils in ordered rock layers provide evidence for when different forms of life appeared and how patterns changed over time.
questions.explanation: This links rock order, fossil evidence, and careful claims.

questions.prompt: Which investigation would deepen a fossil claim?
questions.questionText: Which investigation would deepen a fossil claim?
options: Ignore the layer labels.
Choose the fossil with the coolest name.
Use only one unlocated fossil.
Compare the same fossil pattern in several undisturbed rock sequences.
questions.correctAnswer: Compare the same fossil pattern in several undisturbed rock sequences.
questions.explanation: Repeating the pattern strengthens the claim.
